description: More lawful ways to keep a Georgia child injury settlement under the $25,000 net threshold: structured payments, court-approved trusts, liens and more.
shortAnswer: The key is the “net settlement.” It is the gross settlement minus attorney’s fees and expenses, enforceable liens, money the child will receive after reaching adulthood, and money placed in a court-approved trust. Used well, they can keep the net settlement at $25,000 or less, which keeps a conservatorship out of your family’s life.

sections.heading: What the law lets you subtract
sections.shortAnswer: In 2022 the legislature rewrote the settlement statute. Each of those is a tool. Used well, they can keep the net settlement at $25,000 or less.

sections.heading: Strategy 1: Pay the child later, on purpose
sections.shortAnswer: Money that will be paid to your child after the child becomes an adult is subtracted from the net settlement. A structured settlement does not have to be all or nothing.

sections.heading: Strategy 2: Put the money in a court-approved trust
sections.shortAnswer: Money placed in a trust for the child’s benefit, approved or created by the court, is also subtracted from the net settlement. If a lawsuit is pending, the judge in that case can approve the settlement and order the money paid directly into the trust.

sections.heading: Strategy 3: Settle the parents’ claim separately, and honestly
sections.shortAnswer: The parents’ claim does not need a judge’s approval. The split has to follow the real losses.

sections.heading: Strategy 4: Resolve the liens before you sign
sections.shortAnswer: A lien that is legally enforceable against the settlement is subtracted from the net settlement. Negotiate the liens down first.

sections.heading: Strategy 5: Choose the right court
sections.shortAnswer: If no lawsuit has been filed, the petition goes to the probate court. If a lawsuit is pending, the court where it is pending has exclusive jurisdiction to approve the settlement.

sections.heading: What none of this avoids
sections.shortAnswer: If the gross settlement is more than $25,000, a judge still has to approve it before it binds your child. That rule protects families.

sections.heading: What I tell parents
sections.shortAnswer: Do not agree to a number until you know how it will be paid. Ask about a trust or a structured settlement if the net amount will be over $25,000.

faq.q: When does a Georgia child injury settlement require a conservator?
faq.a: If the net settlement is over $25,000, a judge must approve the settlement, and a conservator must be appointed to receive the money. If the gross settlement is over $25,000 but the net settlement is $25,000 or less, a judge must approve it, but no conservator is needed.

faq.q: Can a child's settlement be paid into a trust instead of a conservatorship in Georgia?
faq.a: Money placed in a trust for the child’s benefit, approved or created by the court, is subtracted from the net settlement. When the money goes straight from the insurer into the trust, no conservatorship is required, because the parent never receives it. Not every court reads it the same way.

faq.q: Does a structured settlement reduce the net settlement for a minor in Georgia?
faq.a: Yes. Money that will be paid to your child after the child becomes an adult is subtracted from the net settlement. Many families structure most of the money to begin at 18, and take a smaller amount now.

faq.q: Which court approves a minor's settlement in Georgia?
faq.a: If no lawsuit has been filed, the petition to approve the settlement goes to the probate court. If a lawsuit is pending, the court where it is pending has exclusive jurisdiction to approve the settlement.
